Spinning and then making khadi cloth would provide them enough clothes for their own use. It would also teach Indians dignity of labour. markup: Write the paragraph on the following topic: Kabaddi
answermarkup: Kabaddi Kabaddi is an ancient sport which originated in India. It has now become popular in many countries and is a part of many international events these days. While in these competitions international rules are followed, various Kabaddi styles are followed in different parts of India In Kabaddi, two teams of seven players each face each other on a flat, rectangular court, which is divided by a mid-line. The game is usually played in two halves with a halftime, break in between, after which the teams exchange their sides in the court. To play this game, each team sends 'raiders across the mid-line to the other team. The 'raider' tries to 'tag' the opponents and run back all in one breath. To show that he hasn't inhaled again, he has to chant 'kabaddi-kabaddi' continuously In case, the player inhales again, he is 'out'. The opponents try to catch the "raider' and stop him from going back to his half till he loses his breath and has to inhale again. If the player manages to get back to his half successfully, all the players he has tagged and all those who have touched him are declared 'out'. For each player who is declared out, the opposite team scores a point. In case, all seven players in a team are 'out', the opposite team scores bonus points. The team with the maximum points wins the match. The game of Kabaddi requires good health, muscular strength strategic skills and a lot of practice. Kabaddi is the National Sport of India.

markup: Have you ever given up on something good? Share your story.
answermarkup: THE DAY I GAVE UP I remember the day clearly. I was not even eight years old. I had been going for karate classes since two months. Unfortunately, the coach was extremely strict and grumpy. If we forgot some move or were absent even once, he made us do the frog jump. This was not only exhausting but also humiliating. I began to develop a dislike for the coach, who never praised any of us or showed any appreciation. He was always impatient and in a hurry to go to his next coaching session. I began to cry every Tuesday and Friday, just before the time when I had to leave for the class. In fact, I even began to fall sick. My mother realized that something was wrong, and she questioned me. When I explained to her, she said that I must persevere and not give up. However, I had developed such a dislike for karate and for the coach that I refused to continue. I turned stubborn, and my mother finally gave up. I stopped going for the classes. Now, when I see my friends doing karate moves, I regret that I gave up and did not continue with the coaching. Maybe I will get a chance sometime in the future.

markup: Write essays on the following topic: The Accident
answermarkup: The Accident Nobody knows what will happen a moment later... The truth of this statement is reflected in the tale I am about to narrate. This incident took place a couple of years ago but I still find it difficult to get it out of my mind. It all began with a harmless plan for a short holiday with family and friends. Our parents readily agreed to go to Lonavala. It was decided that my friend Sanjay's family chauffeur, Mohan Chacha would drive us there and back. With all the plans in place, a day was decided and soon we set off early in the morning, so that Mohan Chacha could drive slowly and still reach at a decent hour. Our parents kept calling almost every half hour to make sure we were safe. Soon we reached and spent two lovely days at a holiday resort. We left after breakfast and should have been home in a few hours but that was where things began to go wrong. While on the highway, a truck came charging at us out of nowhere, at breakneck speed. Mohan Chacha tried to veer the car, but we had the divider beside us. Everything happened so fast, that there was no time to breathe or even blink. All I remember was hearing a loud crash and nothing else. I woke up to the antiseptic smell of the hospital. When my vision cleared, I realised that my family was there too. I tried to look around for my friends but my entire body was injured and 1 could not move. I was told that though my friends were hurt, they were alright. However, Mohan Chacha was critically wounded and so was the driver of the truck that hit us. Apparently, his brakes had failed causing him to lose control. We were discharged from the hospital in a couple of days and left nursing minor injuries. Unfortunately neither Mohan Chacha nor the driver of the truck made it.... What started as a fun filled holiday for us ended in a critical disaster that none of us would forget. There were lives lost and people wounded, and there was really nobody to blame What if we had not made this plan? What if we had not gone to Lonavala? But there was no point in thinking about that anymore... none of these questions had any answers. Our lives had changed in that or moment, and forever. I have since then, never been very comfortable with the idea of a long drive anymore.
